02-flamingo.name: Flamingo One Leg
02-flamingo.idea: Flamingos sleep on one leg because their body locks into place with almost no muscle effort.
02-flamingo.title: Why flamingos stand on ONE leg (it's the lazy option)
02-flamingo.hook: Standing on one leg looks hard. For a flamingo it's the easy way.
02-flamingo.body: In 2017, scientists found a flamingo's body locks into a stable one-leg pose with almost no muscle work. Even a dead flamingo balanced on one leg. Two legs actually take more effort.
sources: The Conversation (Georgia Tech / Emory study, Biology Letters 2017) https://theconversation.com/scientists-balanced-a-dead-flamingo-on-one-leg-to-unlock-the-birds-standing-secret-78231
Science News Explores https://www.snexplores.org/article/how-flamingo-balances-one-leg

03-plane-windows.name: Plane Windows
03-plane-windows.idea: Plane windows are rounded because square corners concentrate stress, which helped break apart the de Havilland Comet in 1954.
03-plane-windows.title: Why plane windows are NEVER square
03-plane-windows.hook: The first jet airliner had square windows. It did not end well.
03-plane-windows.body: In 1954 two de Havilland Comets broke apart mid-air. Tests in a giant water tank showed cracks growing from the sharp window corners, where stress piles up. Rounded corners spread that stress out evenly.
sources: HowStuffWorks: Why are airplane windows round? https://science.howstuffworks.com/transport/flight/modern/airplane-windows-round.htm
Migflug: de Havilland Comet, metal fatigue and square windows https://migflug.com/afterburner/de/de-havilland-comet-first-jet-airliner-metal-fatigue-square-windows/

04-venus.name: Venus Hottest Planet
04-venus.idea: Venus is hotter than Mercury because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat.
04-venus.title: Mercury is closer to the Sun. So why is Venus HOTTER?
04-venus.hook: The closest planet to the Sun is not the hottest one.
04-venus.body: Mercury has almost no air, so its heat escapes to space. Venus is wrapped in thick carbon dioxide that traps the heat. Its surface stays above 460°C, day and night. Hot enough to melt lead.
sources: NASA Space Place: All about Venus https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/all-about-venus/en/
BBC Sky at Night: Why is Venus the hottest planet? https://skyatnightmagazine.com/space-science/venus-hottest-planet

05-woodpecker.name: Woodpecker No Concussion
05-woodpecker.idea: Woodpecker skulls are not shock absorbers; their tiny brains simply tolerate the jolts.
05-woodpecker.title: Woodpeckers hit trees all day. Why no concussion?
05-woodpecker.hook: Bang your head on a tree like this and you'd be knocked out.
05-woodpecker.body: For years people thought a woodpecker's skull was a shock absorber. A 2022 high-speed camera study found the opposite: the head works like a stiff hammer. The real secret is size. A tiny brain can take much bigger jolts.
sources: Smithsonian Magazine https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/woodpecker-skulls-dont-absorb-shock-like-previously-thought-180980426/
Van Wassenbergh et al., Current Biology 2022 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2022.05.052

06-wrinkly-fingers.name: Wrinkly Fingers
06-wrinkly-fingers.idea: Bath-wrinkled fingers are switched on by your nervous system, possibly to improve grip on wet things.
06-wrinkly-fingers.title: Your wrinkly bath fingers are NOT just soggy skin
06-wrinkly-fingers.hook: Those prune fingers after a bath? Your nerves are doing that.
06-wrinkly-fingers.body: If the nerve to a finger is damaged, that finger stays smooth. Your nervous system shrinks blood vessels under the skin and pulls it into ridges. One idea: grip. In tests people handled wet objects better with wrinkly fingers.
sources: Popular Science: Why do fingers wrinkle in water? https://www.popsci.com/science/why-do-fingers-wrinkle-in-water/
USC: Wrinkly fingertips proven useful https://scribe.usc.edu/weird-science-wrinkly-fingertips-proven-useful/

07-astronaut-bones.name: Astronaut Bones
07-astronaut-bones.idea: Astronauts lose bone in space because bones rebuild based on the load they carry.
07-astronaut-bones.title: Space slowly eats astronauts' bones. Here's why
07-astronaut-bones.hook: Astronauts float with no weight. So why do they come home weaker?
07-astronaut-bones.body: Your bones rebuild themselves based on the load they carry. In space your legs and hips carry almost nothing, so the body takes bone away, around 1 to 2 percent a month. That's why space station crews exercise every single day.
sources: NASA Astrobiology: Space bones https://astrobiology.nasa.gov/nai/articles/2001/10/10/space-bones/index.html
Universe Today: NASA learns more about bone loss in space https://universetoday.com/9380/nasa-learns-more-about-bone-loss-in-space

08-sixty-minutes.name: Sixty Minutes
08-sixty-minutes.idea: An hour has 60 minutes because the Babylonians counted in base 60, which divides evenly many ways.
08-sixty-minutes.title: Why does an hour have 60 minutes, not 100?
08-sixty-minutes.hook: 100 minutes in an hour would be easier. So why 60?
08-sixty-minutes.body: Blame the Babylonians. They counted in sixties, and 60 splits evenly into halves, thirds, quarters, fifths, sixths and tenths. Their astronomers used it to track the sky and time. We still use it for hours, minutes, seconds and the 360 degrees of a circle.
sources: Think Academy: Why does an hour have 60 minutes? https://www.thethinkacademy.com/blog/edubriefs-why-does-an-hour-have-60-minutes-explained-with-history-and-math/
The Star: The ancient reason there are 60 minutes in an hour https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/world/2026-03-29-the-ancient-reason-there-are-60-minutes-in-an-hour

09-spider-web.name: Spider Web
09-spider-web.idea: Spiders avoid sticking to their own webs thanks to branching leg hairs, a non-stick coating and careful movement.
09-spider-web.title: Why spiders don't get stuck in their own webs
09-spider-web.hook: A web traps flies. So why doesn't the spider get stuck?
09-spider-web.body: In 2012 Smithsonian researchers looked closely at spider legs. Branching hairs mean only a few tips touch the glue, and the legs carry a non-stick coating. Wash it off and the legs stick much more. Spiders also move carefully.
sources: Smithsonian Science: Fancy footwork and non-stick leg coating https://smithsonianscience.org/2012/03/fancy-footwork-and-non-stick-leg-coating-helps-spiders-not-stick-to-their-own-webs/
Phys.org: Why spiders do not stick to their own webs https://phys.org/news/2012-03-spiders-sticky-web-sites.html

10-ice-floats.name: Ice Floats
10-ice-floats.idea: Ice floats because water molecules lock into a roomy crystal when frozen, making ice less dense than water.
10-ice-floats.title: Ice SHOULD sink. Here's why it floats
10-ice-floats.hook: Almost everything sinks when it freezes solid. Not water.
10-ice-floats.body: When water freezes, its molecules lock into a roomy crystal, so ice is lighter than the same amount of water. Lakes freeze from the top down, and the ice works like a lid that keeps the water below liquid all winter. Lucky fish.
sources: UC ANR: Why does ice float? https://ucanr.edu/node/155410
Why lakes and ponds freeze from the top down https://www.dl-online.com/weather/why-lakes-and-ponds-freeze-from-the-top-down

11-leap-year.name: Leap Year
11-leap-year.idea: Leap years exist because Earth's orbit takes about 365.25 days; most century years skip it to fix the overshoot.
11-leap-year.title: Why February 29 exists (and why 1900 skipped it)
11-leap-year.hook: Why does February get an extra day every four years?
11-leap-year.body: Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to orbit the Sun. Skip that quarter and the calendar slips almost a day every four years, more than three weeks a century. Adding February 29 overshoots a little, so most century years skip it.
sources: Royal Museums Greenwich: Which years are leap years? https://www.rmg.co.uk/discover/explore/which-years-are-leap-years-and-can-you-have-leap-seconds
Astronomy.com: Why do we have leap days? https://www.astronomy.com/observing/why-do-we-have-leap-days-this-week-in-astronomy-with-dave-eicher/
